directions: Rosecoco is one of Kenya's most widely grown and traded dry bean market classes, prized for its large cream-colored seeds mottled with rose-pink streaks and its creamy texture once cooked into githeri or plain boiled beans. Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, spacing plants to allow good air movement, since humid conditions can favor foliar disease in this upright bush grower. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before shelling, as the distinctive speckled seed coat is a hallmark of properly cured Rosecoco beans sold in East African markets. Rotate with cereal crops in the garden to help manage soil-borne bean pathogens.
sources: Pan-Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA) Kenya bean market class reports
Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) common bean variety guides

directions: Gadam is a short-season, drought-hardy white grain sorghum widely grown by smallholder farmers in Kenya's semi-arid eastern counties, where it has become an important cash crop supplying regional malting and brewing demand as well as home milling into flour and porridge. It tolerates erratic rainfall and poor soils far better than maize, still setting a compact grain head on a sturdy stalk in dry years that would cause maize to fail outright. Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger passes, thin to a wide spacing to reduce competition for scarce moisture, and net or guard the heads against birds as the grain ripens to a pale, starchy color. Harvest once heads are fully dry, then thresh and store the grain in a cool, dry place.
sources: Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) sorghum variety releases
International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT)

directions: Katumani Composite was bred at Kenya's national dryland research station in Katumani, Machakos, to give smallholder farmers in drought-prone semi-arid lowlands a maize that could set a harvestable cob before short, erratic rains cut off. Its defining trait is speed to maturity, reaching harvest well ahead of standard dent or flint maize and letting growers dodge mid-season dry spells that would otherwise cause total crop loss. Because it is an open-pollinated composite rather than a hybrid, farmers can save and replant seed from a reasonably uniform crop, which matters where fresh hybrid seed is not affordable or available every season. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil and expect smaller ears than long-season hybrids in exchange for reliable drought resilience.
sources: Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) Katumani Research Centre variety history
FAO East Africa drought-tolerant maize program reports

planting.note: Plant a sucker or tissue-cultured division after frost danger passes in rich, constantly moist, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Mbwazirume is one of the most widely planted East African Highland cooking banana cultivars in Uganda, valued by farmers for its large bunches and better tolerance of the leaf-spot diseases that trouble many Cavendish-type bananas in the region. Unlike dessert bananas, its starchy green fruit is peeled and steamed whole, then mashed into the staple dish known as matoke rather than eaten fresh. It is a tall, vigorous triploid highland banana that needs rich, constantly moist soil and heavy mulching to support its thick pseudostem and heavy fruit bunch. Grow it in full sun in a warm, frost-free climate, and remove excess suckers so the plant channels its energy into one main stem and a single follow-on sucker.
sources: ProMusa (Bioversity International/CIRAD) East African Highland banana cultivar descriptions

planting.note: Plant a sucker or tissue-cultured division after frost danger passes in deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun.

directions: Kibuzi is a traditional Ugandan highland cooking banana grown for matoke, recognized locally by its more slender, finger-like fruit compared with the plumper Nfuuka-group cultivars typically grown for commercial sale. Like other East African Highland bananas, it is a triploid clone propagated only from suckers or tissue-cultured plantlets rather than seed, and it is one of hundreds of locally named cultivars maintained in Ugandan home gardens over many generations. The plant forms a tall, dense clump of broad paddle-shaped leaves above a thick pseudostem marked with the dark blotches typical of this banana group. Provide deep, fertile, consistently moist soil, full sun, and some wind shelter, and expect the first bunch roughly a year after planting a sucker.
sources: ProMusa (Bioversity International/CIRAD) East African Highland banana cultivar descriptions
Bioversity International Musa Germplasm Information System

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and set out plants after frost danger passes against a sturdy trellis or fence in full sun.

directions: Loroco is a twining, milky-sapped vine native to the dry tropical forests of Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras, grown not for fruit but for its small, fragrant, still-unopened flower buds, which are hand-picked and used to flavor pupusas, tamales, scrambled eggs, and rice throughout the region's Mayan-rooted culinary tradition. It is typically propagated from stem cuttings rather than seed, since the species remains only partially domesticated and seed germination is slow and inconsistent. Give it a sturdy trellis or fence to climb, warm frost-free conditions, and well-drained soil, and expect the vine to need a full growing season to establish before it settles into steady bud production. Harvest the tight, unopened flower clusters regularly through the warm months to encourage the vine to keep producing.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension notes on Central American tropical vegetables
USDA ARS Germplasm Resources Information Network (GRIN)
